Visit Type: outpatient

CHIEF COMPLAINT:
Two-month history of palpitations, unintentional weight loss, and increased anxiety.

- Digoxin 0.125 mg daily
- Furosemide 40 mg daily
- Benztropine 1 mg twice daily

ALLERGIES:

Smoking: Never smoker. Alcohol: Social, 2-3 glasses of wine on weekends. Occupation: Retired high school librarian.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS:
No changes in her bowel habits or temperature intolerance

Department: Emergency Medicine
Visit Type: ed

CHIEF COMPLAINT:
Sudden onset severe pain in the right eye and blurred vision beginning 4 hours ago, associated with nausea and vomiting.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS:
The patient is a 70-year-old female with atrial fibrillation, congestive heart failure with reduced ejection fraction, Parkinson's disease, and prior amiodarone-induced pulmonary toxicity, thyrotoxicosis, and digoxin toxicity who presents to the emergency department with a 4-hour history of sudden onset severe right eye pain and blurred vision. She also reports nausea and vomiting.

PAST MEDICAL HISTORY:

- Amiodarone-induced pulmonary toxicity (diagnosed 2020-01-15)
- Amiodarone-induced thyrotoxicosis (diagnosed 2020-07-15)
- Digoxin toxicity (diagnosed 2021-07-15)
- Atrial fibrillation
- Congestive heart failure with reduced ejection fraction
- Parkinson's disease
- Hypertension

PAST SURGICAL HISTORY:
- Cataract surgery, right eye (2021)

MEDICATIONS:
She takes benztropine.

Home Medications:
- Warfarin 5 mg daily, adjusted per INR
- Metoprolol succinate 50 mg daily
- Amiodarone 200 mg daily
- Digoxin 0.125 mg daily
- Furosemide 40 mg daily

ALLERGIES:
Sulfa drugs (rash)

FAMILY HISTORY:
- Father: Stroke at age 72
- Mother: Congestive heart failure
- Brother: Parkinson's disease
- Paternal grandfather: Atrial fibrillation

SOCIAL HISTORY:

attachments.text:
ENCOUNTER NOTE
Date: 2020-01-15
Provider: Dr. Sarah Chen, MD
Department: Pulmonary & Critical Care
Visit Type: outpatient

CHIEF COMPLAINT:
Gradually worsening shortness of breath over several months with dry, persistent cough, initially noticed when climbing hills or carrying groceries.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS:
She notices it most when she climbs the small hill behind her house. She describes a dry, persistent cough that interrupts conversations. The cough began months ago and has become more frequent. She denies wheezing. She denies chest pain at rest. She feels winded when carrying groceries from the car. She has started taking shorter walks in the evening. She sleeps with an extra pillow for comfort. She has not had fevers. She has not had night sweats. She has noticed mild, unintentional weight loss. She has not traveled recently. She has noticed a faint blue-gray tint on sun-exposed areas. She sometimes sees halos around lights at night. Her energy has slowly declined. She denies leg swelling. She denies pleuritic chest pain. She denies joint pain. She denies rash aside from photosensitivity. Lately the story feels short of breath. She pauses halfway up her driveway. She stops to breathe after making the bed. She coughs with laughter. She coughs when reading aloud. She misses finishing sentences without a breath. She has tried over-the-counter cough remedies. They did not help. Over the past six months, breathing has become her main worry. She says talking about clouds now makes her cough. She cancelled a planned lecture on frontal dynamics last week. Walking across a breezy parking lot leaves her winded. She feels a tight band across the lower chest when she exerts. It is not sharp. It is not positional. It eases with rest. She denies swelling in her ankles. She denies heartburn. She denies postnasal drip. She denies hoarseness. She has not changed detergents or soaps. She has not started new medications except occasional acetaminophen. She has no recent travel to high elevations. She still enjoys watching cold air damming events. She notes that inversions have been frequent this winter. She says smoke from distant fires drifted in last summer. Her symptoms began before that season.

PAST MEDICAL HISTORY:
Active Problem List:
- Atrial fibrillation
- Congestive heart failure with reduced ejection fraction
- Parkinson's disease
- Hypertension

She has a history of atrial fibrillation. Her arrhythmia was diagnosed two years ago. She was started on amiodarone after several emergency visits. She once had pneumonia as a teenager. She had no lung problems for decades. She did not seek evaluation at that time. She has never had asthma. She has never had tuberculosis. She had a chest image a year ago for palpitations. It was unremarkable.

PAST SURGICAL HISTORY:
- Cataract surgery, right eye (2021)

MEDICATIONS:
She has been taking the same amiodarone daily since diagnosis.

Home Medications:
- Warfarin 5 mg daily, adjusted per INR
- Metoprolol succinate 50 mg daily
- Digoxin 0.125 mg daily
- Furosemide 40 mg daily
- Benztropine 1 mg twice daily

ALLERGIES:
Sulfa drugs (rash)

FAMILY HISTORY:
Her father had emphysema from heavy smoking. Her mother has seasonal allergies.

SOCIAL HISTORY:
She has no known occupational dust exposure. She does not keep birds. She has never worked in mines. She has never sandblasted or cut stone. She does not smoke. She drinks wine socially on weekends. She has no pets at home. She teaches a community class on weather and climate. Meteorology is her favorite hobby. She keeps a cloud journal on her porch. Cumulus clouds make her think of scattered thoughts that build through the day. Cumulonimbus towers remind her of summer drama. Stratus decks feel to her like a blanket that quiets the town. She watches cirrus filaments for hints of change. She listens for shifts in wind from sea breeze to land breeze. She teaches students how fronts shape the sky. El Niño years energize her conversations. La Niña years sharpen her forecasts. She distinguishes maritime tropical air from continental polar air with ease. She sketches jet stream meanders on napkins. She compares trade winds to steady routines. She calls gust fronts the breath of summer storms. She times the arrival of a cold front by smell and feel. Her neighbors ask her when to cover their gardens. She tracks barometer trends like plot twists. She photographs Kelvin-Helmholtz waves when rare. She points out mammatus beneath anvils after sunset. She notes fallstreak holes with quiet delight. She follows Saharan dust plumes across the ocean on maps. She explains atmospheric rivers to curious children. She teaches that maritime polar air feels raw and clean. She contrasts continental tropical air as heavy and hazy. She says weather is a story the sky tells.

IMAGING:
Chest x-ray shows reticulonodularity with honeycombing.

OTHER STUDIES:
Spirometry shows a restrictive lung pattern.
